lab.title: Write the shared Azure settings
lab.text: Every chapter imports this one file, so keep the name `azlab.py` and keep it next to your other files. It reads the simulator address from environment variables and builds the real Azure clients. The management clients (`azure-mgmt-*`) are pointed at the simulator with `base_url`, which is exactly how you point them at a sovereign cloud. The simulator accepts any bearer token on its control plane, so a small fixed-token credential is enough here (on real Azure you would pass `DefaultAzureCredential()`). Later chapters add to the helpers at the bottom, never change the top.
lab.code:
import os
import time
from urllib.parse import urlparse

ENDPOINT = os.environ["VYOMI_AZURE_ENDPOINT"]                          # https://localhost:<port>  (the simulator, TLS with a local CA)
HTTP_ENDPOINT = os.environ.get("VYOMI_AZURE_HTTP_ENDPOINT", ENDPOINT)   # the same simulator on plain http, used by functions and containers
AMQP_PORT = int(os.environ.get("VYOMI_AZURE_AMQP_PORT", "5672"))        # Service Bus AMQP 1.0 listener
SUB = os.environ.get("AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID", "00000000-0000-0000-0000-cloudlearn01")
RG = "rg-facilities"
LOC = "eastus"
TENANT = "facilities-tenant"
HOST = urlparse(ENDPOINT).hostname or "localhost"
STORAGE = "devstoreaccount1"
ACCOUNT_KEY = "Eby8vdM02xNOcqFlqUwJPLlmEtlCDXJ1OUzFT50uSRZ6IFsuFq2UVErCz4I6tq/K1SZFPTOtr/KBHBeksoGMGw=="   # the public Azurite development key
CHAT, EMBED = "chat", "embed"                                            # your deployment names
OPENAI_ACCOUNT = "facilities-openai"

_cache = {}


class DevToken:
    """A TokenCredential that always returns the same development token (the simulator does not check it)."""
    def get_token(self, *scopes, **kwargs):
        from azure.core.credentials import AccessToken
        return AccessToken(os.environ.get("VYOMI_ACCESS_TOKEN", "vyomi-local"), int(time.time()) + 3600)


def arm(cls, **kw):
    """Any azure-mgmt-* client, pointed at the simulator."""
    if cls not in _cache:
        _cache[cls] = cls(DevToken(), SUB, base_url=ENDPOINT, polling_interval=0, **kw)
    return _cache[cls]


def rid(provider, kind, name):
    return f"/subscriptions/{SUB}/resourceGroups/{RG}/providers/{provider}/{kind}/{name}"


def ensure_rg():
    from azure.mgmt.resource.resources import ResourceManagementClient
    arm(ResourceManagementClient).resource_groups.create_or_update(RG, {"location": LOC})


def pick_models():
    """The models are the ones this simulator hosts: in-browser models on Nano, the Mesh model pool on a Mesh. Returns (chat, embedding) as
    the {format, name, version} a deployment needs. Never hard-code a vendor model."""
    from azure.mgmt.cognitiveservices import CognitiveServicesManagementClient
    ms = [{"format": m.model.format, "name": m.model.name, "version": m.model.version} for m in arm(CognitiveServicesManagementClient).models.list(LOC) if m.kind == "OpenAI"]
    emb = [m for m in ms if "embed" in m["name"] or "minilm" in m["name"]]
    return [m for m in ms if m not in emb][0], emb[0]


def aoai(api_version="2024-10-21"):
    from openai import AzureOpenAI
    key = ("aoai", api_version)
    if key not in _cache:
        _cache[key] = AzureOpenAI(azure_endpoint=ENDPOINT, api_key="vyomi-local", api_version=api_version, max_retries=0, timeout=120)
    return _cache[key]

lead: Every layer of the Facilities agent needs a language model, and every layer should reach it the same way. This chapter builds that one door: a small client with three calls, chat, chat with tools and embeddings, that the rest of the course imports.

The models themselves are the open models Vyomi hosts. On Nano they run inside your browser; on a Mesh they come from the Mesh model pool. Your code never hard-codes a model name: it asks the simulator what it hosts and uses what it finds.
concepts: Chat completion
You send a conversation (system instruction plus user turns) and get the next assistant turn back. It is stateless: you resend the history every time.
Tool calling
You describe functions the model may use. The model never runs them: it replies with the name and arguments it wants, your code runs the function and returns the result.
Embedding
A fixed-length list of numbers that places a piece of text in meaning-space. Texts with similar meaning land close together, which is what makes semantic search possible.
Model catalogue
The list of models the platform serves. Reading it at run time keeps your code working when the models behind it change.
flow: List the models the simulator serves and split them into chat and embedding models.
Call the chat API with a user message and read the text and the token usage.
Add a tool definition. The reply is a tool request, not text.
Turn two sentences into vectors and compare them: a paraphrase scores higher than an unrelated sentence.
explain.example: The Facilities agent is asked "What should I do when boiler pressure exceeds 30 psi?". The model layer sends that to the chat model with the boiler tool described. The model answers with a tool request for the asset-status tool, which a later chapter implements.
pitfalls: Hard-coding a model name: it breaks as soon as the platform changes its models.
Treating tool calling as if the model executed the tool. Your code always does the executing.
Mixing embeddings from different models in one index: vectors from different models cannot be compared.

narr.scene: It is 2 a.m. at the Northwind campus. Priya, the night technician, types a question into the new assistant: "Boiler 2 pressure is at 31 psi. What do I do?" Behind that single line, eleven other parts of the system are about to need a language model. If each one connects to a model its own way, the first model change breaks all eleven.
narr.problem: The tempting way is to call a model directly wherever you need one. It works on day one. Then the model changes, a limit changes, or you want to know what the assistant costs, and you are searching the whole codebase.
idea: A power socket

Appliances do not wire themselves into the power station. They plug into a standard socket, and the socket hides what is behind it. The model layer is that socket: three standard calls (chat, chat with tools, embed) that every other layer plugs into.
walk: The platform lists what it hosts

Your code asks which models exist. On Nano the answer is a small model running in your browser; on a Mesh it is a larger one. Your code picks the first chat model and the first embedding model it finds.
Priya's question becomes a chat turn
You send the system instruction ("You are a facilities assistant") and her question. Back comes a sentence and a count of the tokens used.
The model asks for a tool
You also describe a function, asset_status(asset_id). The reply is not text: it is a request, "call asset_status with B-2". The model never runs anything. Your code does.
Meaning becomes numbers
You embed "boiler pressure limit" and "maximum safe steam pressure". The two lists of numbers are close together. "Cafeteria menu" is far away. That distance is how search will work later.
quiz: Priya's agent needs the asset status. Who actually runs the asset_status function?
The model
Your code, after the model asks for it
The cloud provider
Tool calling is a request, never an execution. The model proposes; your code disposes. Everything about safety in later chapters rests on this.
Why does the model layer look up the hosted models instead of hard-coding a name?
It is faster
The models behind the platform can change without your code changing
Names are secret
A hard-coded model name is a hidden dependency. Asking the platform what it hosts keeps every layer working when the models change.
Two sentences have embeddings that are very close. What does that tell you?
They are spelt alike
They have similar meaning
They are the same length
Embeddings place text by meaning, not spelling. That is why a search for "maximum safe steam pressure" can find a page that says "boiler limit".
recap: Every layer talks to models through one small client.
A tool call is a request your code fulfils; the model never runs it.
Embeddings turn meaning into numbers, which makes search by meaning possible.
narr.simple: Call one model directly, by name, from every piece of code that needs it.

Knowing which models the platform actually hosts
One standard way to call tools and to embed text
narr.why: Models change every few months, and each has its own limits, cost and privacy terms. Twelve other layers depend on this one, so a hard-wired model name becomes a risk spread across the whole system.
narr.design: One small client with three standard calls (chat, chat with tools, embed) and a lookup of what the platform hosts. Every other layer plugs into it, so the model can change in one place.

lab.title: Install the libraries
lab.text: Chapter 3 builds the agent runtime. Azure has no single hosted-agent service like AgentCore Runtime or Vertex AI Agent Engine, so this layer is ASSEMBLED from two real services and says so plainly: Azure AI Foundry Agents (`azure-ai-agents`) holds the agent definitions and runs them on threads, and Azure Container Apps (`azure-mgmt-appcontainers`) hosts your own agent code, a LangGraph supervisor, behind an HTTPS ingress. It relies on the chat deployment from chapter 10 and `azlab.py`.

lab.title: Create the supervisor and the three sub-agents in Foundry
lab.text: Four agent definitions in the Foundry project `facilities-project`, created with the real `azure-ai-agents` client: a supervisor that routes, and Facilities, Maintenance and Analytics sub-agents. The tool definitions are declared now (the model can ask for them); chapter 7 builds the tools themselves and chapter 4 puts a gateway in front of them. Then the supervisor runs on a thread: create thread, add a user message, create a run, poll it. The model is the repo's deterministic test stub: it answers a question that mentions tools by asking for one, so the run stops in `requires_action` (the model asked your code to call a tool and is waiting). That is the correct, expected state here: chapter 7 builds the tools and chapter 4 the gateway they sit behind.
lab.code:
import time
from azure.ai.agents import AgentsClient
from azlab import ENDPOINT, DevToken, CHAT

client = AgentsClient(endpoint=f"{ENDPOINT}/api/projects/facilities-project", credential=DevToken())

TOOLS = [
    {"type": "function", "function": {"name": "kb_search", "description": "Search the facilities knowledge base (read-only).",
        "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"query": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["query"]}}},
    {"type": "function", "function": {"name": "asset_status", "description": "Look up an asset and its work orders (read-only).",
        "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"asset_id": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["asset_id"]}}},
    {"type": "function", "function": {"name": "create_work_order", "description": "Request a work order (needs human approval).",
        "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"asset_id": {"type": "string"}, "summary": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["asset_id", "summary"]}}},
]
AGENTS = (("facilities_supervisor", "You route facilities requests to the Facilities, Maintenance and Analytics agents and combine their answers.", TOOLS),
          ("facilities_facilities", "Answer from the knowledge base only, with citations.", TOOLS[:1]),
          ("facilities_maintenance", "Look up assets and raise work orders (approval required).", TOOLS[1:]),
          ("facilities_analytics", "Count and summarise work orders.", []))
ids = {}
for name, instructions, tools in AGENTS:
    ids[name] = client.create_agent(model=CHAT, name=name, instructions=instructions, tools=tools).id
print("agents:", sorted(a.name for a in client.list_agents() if a.name in ids))

thread = client.threads.create()
client.messages.create(thread_id=thread.id, role="user", content="Boiler B-12 is at 34 psi. What does the SOP say?")
run = client.runs.create(thread_id=thread.id, agent_id=ids["facilities_supervisor"])
for _ in range(60):
    run = client.runs.get(thread_id=thread.id, run_id=run.id)
    if str(run.status).lower().split(".")[-1] not in ("queued", "in_progress"):
        break
    time.sleep(0.5)
print("supervisor run:", str(run.status).lower().split(".")[-1], "| messages on the thread:", len(list(client.messages.list(thread_id=thread.id))))

lab.title: Write the supervisor graph
lab.text: The agent code itself, a LangGraph `StateGraph`: the supervisor asks the model which sub-agents are needed (a JSON list), runs them in order, and synthesises one answer. Each sub-agent is a node with its own role prompt. Every span (a timed step) is recorded in the state, because chapter 8 turns them into traces. At this point the sub-agents have no tools (those arrive in chapters 7 and 4), so each answers from the model alone: that is stated in the code, not hidden. The cloud is injected as a `converse(system, text)` function, so this file has no Azure code in it and is reused unchanged in later chapters.
lab.code:
import json
import re
import time
from typing import TypedDict
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, END

ROUTER_PROMPT = (
    "You route facilities requests to specialist agents. The agents are:\n"
    "- facilities: searches the knowledge base (SOPs, safety rules, policies, maintenance procedures, how-to guidance).\n"
    "- maintenance: looks up a specific asset (ids like B-12 or AHU-7) and its work orders, and can raise a work order.\n"
    "- analytics: counts and statistics over work orders (how many, trends, summaries).\n"
    "Pick every agent needed. Reply with only a JSON list such as [\"facilities\",\"maintenance\"], drawn from [\"facilities\",\"maintenance\",\"analytics\"]."
)
ROLES = {"facilities": "You are the Facilities agent. Answer procedure and safety questions.",
         "maintenance": "You are the Maintenance agent. Answer questions about assets and work orders.",
         "analytics": "You are the Analytics agent. Answer questions that need counts or summaries."}


class State(TypedDict, total=False):
    question: str
    user: str
    route: list
    notes: dict
    citations: list
    approval: str
    answer: str
    llm_used: bool
    spans: list


def build(converse, tools=None):
    """converse(system, text) -> str. tools: optional {name: callable}; sub-agents use a tool when one is supplied (chapters 7 and 4 supply them)."""
    tools = tools or {}

    def span(st, name, t0):
        st.setdefault("spans", []).append({"name": name, "kind": "agent", "start": t0, "end": time.time()})

    def supervisor(st):
        t0 = time.time()
        plan = None
        text = converse(ROUTER_PROMPT, st["question"])
        try:
            plan = [p for p in json.loads(re.search(r"\[.*\]", text, re.S).group(0)) if p in ROLES]
        except Exception:
            plan = None
        st["llm_used"] = bool(plan)
        st["route"] = plan or ["facilities"]
        st["notes"] = {}
        span(st, "supervisor.plan", t0)
        return st

    def sub_agent(name):
        def node(st):
            t0 = time.time()
            if name in tools:
                st["notes"][name] = tools[name](st)
            else:
                st["notes"][name] = converse(ROLES[name], st["question"])
            span(st, f"agent:{name}", t0)
            return st
        return node

    def synthesize(st):
        t0 = time.time()
        context = "\n".join(f"[{i + 1}] {n}" for i, n in enumerate(st["notes"].values()))
        st["answer"] = converse("Answer using only the context. Cite sources like [1].", f"Context:\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {st['question']}")
        span(st, "supervisor.synthesize", t0)
        return st

    g = StateGraph(State)
    g.add_node("supervisor", supervisor)
    for n in ROLES:
        g.add_node(n, sub_agent(n))
    g.add_node("synth", synthesize)
    g.set_entry_point("supervisor")
    order = list(ROLES)

    def next_after(after):
        def pick(st):
            rest = [a for a in (order[order.index(after) + 1:] if after else order) if a in st["route"]]
            return rest[0] if rest else "synth"
        return pick
    targets = {**{n: n for n in order}, "synth": "synth"}
    for src in ["supervisor"] + order:
        g.add_conditional_edges(src, next_after(None if src == "supervisor" else src), targets)
    g.add_edge("synth", END)
    return g.compile()

lab.title: Create the Container Apps environment and the app
lab.text: Two ARM calls with `azure-mgmt-appcontainers`: a managed environment, then the container app `facilities-supervisor` with external ingress on port 8080. The simulator's Python app image `vyomi/python-app:latest` starts `app.py` from the zip you pass in `VYOMI_APP_SOURCE_B64`; on real Azure you would instead build a container image from the same two files, push it to Azure Container Registry and put its name in `image`. The environment variables are the endpoint the container calls the model on, the same way you would set them on real Container Apps.

import os
import zipfile
from azure.mgmt.appcontainers import ContainerAppsAPIClient
from azlab import arm, rid, RG, LOC, HTTP_ENDPOINT

    "configuration": {"ingress": {"external": True, "targetPort": 8080}},

        {"name": "VYOMI_APP_SOURCE_B64", "value": bundle}, {"name": "VYOMI_ENDPOINT", "value": HTTP_ENDPOINT}]}]}}}).result()

lab.title: Call the hosted supervisor in two sessions
lab.text: Read the ingress address from the container app (the simulator reports it as `vyomiIngressUrl`; on real Azure it is `properties.configuration.ingress.fqdn`) and `POST /query`. Session `s1` asks twice and session `s2` once: the turn counters prove the two sessions do not share history. The hosted app runs the LangGraph supervisor and sub-agents inside the container process (see the `pid`).
lab.code:
import requests
from azure.mgmt.appcontainers import ContainerAppsAPIClient
from azlab import arm, RG

raw = arm(ContainerAppsAPIClient).container_apps.get(RG, "facilities-supervisor", cls=lambda resp, des, hdr: resp.http_response.json())
base = raw["properties"]["vyomiIngressUrl"].rstrip("/")


def ask(session, prompt):
    r = requests.post(base + "/query", json={"prompt": prompt, "user": "maria", "session": session}, timeout=60)
    r.raise_for_status()

lead: An agent is a loop: read the request, decide what to do, call tools, read the results, decide again. The runtime is the place that loop lives. It also decides what happens when the loop misbehaves: how many steps, how many tokens, how long.
In this chapter you build a supervisor that plans and routes work to three specialists, Facilities, Maintenance and Analytics, and you host it so that every user session is isolated from every other.
concepts: Supervisor and sub-agents
One agent plans and delegates; narrow specialists each do one kind of work. Narrow agents are easier to test and to restrict.
Agent harness
The limits around the loop: step budget, token budget, cost ceiling, timeouts and a kill switch. Without it a confused agent can run up cost indefinitely.
Session
One conversation with one user. State, memory and budgets belong to a session and must never leak into another.
Checkpoint
A saved snapshot of the agent's progress, so a long task can resume after a failure.
flow: The supervisor reads the question and decides which specialists are needed.
Each specialist handles its part, using the tools you build in the next chapters.
The supervisor merges the specialist answers into one reply.
The runtime keeps a separate state for each session id, so two users never see each other's data.
explain.example: A question about a failing air handler needs the SOP (Facilities), the asset's maintenance history (Maintenance) and the energy trend (Analytics). The supervisor calls all three and writes one answer. A second user asking at the same time gets a completely separate session.
pitfalls: One giant agent with every tool: hard to test and impossible to restrict.
No step or token budget: a loop that never converges becomes a bill.
Storing session state in a global variable: sessions bleed into each other.

narr.scene: Priya's next question is bigger: "AHU-7 is drifting hot. Is it the valve, and when was it last serviced?" No single skill answers that. It needs the procedure, the maintenance history and the energy trend, three different kinds of work.
narr.problem: One giant agent with every tool tries to be an expert in everything. It gets slow, confused and hard to test. And when two users talk to it at once, their conversations can bleed into each other.
idea: A head chef and a line of cooks

The head chef does not chop, grill and plate. They read the order, give each cook their part and assemble the dish. The supervisor agent plans and delegates; Facilities, Maintenance and Analytics each do one thing well.
walk: The supervisor reads the question
"Drifting hot" and "last serviced" tell it it needs the SOP, the history and the trend.
Three specialists each take a part
Facilities finds the procedure. Maintenance finds the service record for AHU-7. Analytics reads the energy trend.
The supervisor writes one answer
It merges the three results into a single reply with a recommended next step.
The runtime keeps sessions apart
Priya's conversation has its own session id, state and budget. A second technician asking at the same moment cannot see or disturb it.
quiz: Why split the work between a supervisor and specialists?
It looks tidy
Narrow agents are easier to test, restrict and reason about
It uses fewer tokens always
Specialists with a small job and few tools are predictable. You can test each one and give it only the access it needs.
What is a step or token budget for?
Billing reports
Stopping an agent that loops without converging
Making answers longer
Without a limit a confused agent can keep calling tools and models indefinitely. The harness is what turns a runaway into a stopped, logged failure.
Two users ask at the same time. What must be true?
They share state to save memory
Each session has isolated state
The second waits for the first
Session isolation is a security property, not a performance feature. Shared state is how one user's data reaches another.
recap: A supervisor plans and delegates; specialists each do one job.
The harness (budgets, timeouts, a kill switch) is what makes an agent safe to run.
Every session is isolated from every other.
narr.simple: One agent holding every tool, looping until it decides it is finished.
got: Fine for one user at a time
missing: A limit on steps, time and spend
Separation between two users' sessions
Small specialists you can test and restrict one by one
narr.why: An unbounded loop spends real money, and shared state is how one user's data reaches another. An enterprise has to be able to say what the agent may do, for how long, for whom.
narr.design: A supervisor that plans and delegates to specialists, inside a harness with budgets, timeouts and a kill switch, and with every session isolated.

import json
import os
import azure.functions as func


def main(req: func.HttpRequest) -> func.HttpResponse:
    from azure.core.credentials import AzureKeyCredential
    from azure.search.documents import SearchClient
    body = req.get_json() if req.get_body() else {}
    sc = SearchClient(os.environ["SEARCH_ENDPOINT"], os.environ.get("SEARCH_INDEX", "facilities-kb"), AzureKeyCredential(os.environ["SEARCH_KEY"]))

lead: Tools are how an agent touches the real world. A tool is an ordinary function with a strict contract: what it accepts, what it returns, what it is allowed to do. The agent is only ever as safe as the tools you hand it.
You will build read-only tools first, a knowledge search and an asset-status lookup, and then the write tools, request-approval and create-work-order, that must sit behind a human decision.
concepts: Tool contract
A typed input, a typed output and a clear description. The model reads the description to decide when to call the tool.
Read-only versus write
Reads can be retried and run freely. Writes change the world, so they are gated, logged and made idempotent.
Least privilege
Each tool gets only the permissions it needs: the asset lookup can read one table and nothing else.
Never trust the caller
The arguments come from a model. Validate every input in the tool, as you would for any untrusted request.
flow: Create the tables for assets, work orders and the approval ledger, and seed a few rows.
Deploy kb-search and asset-status as functions.
Deploy request-approval and create-work-order. They do not write directly: they hand off to approval.
Call every tool directly and check what comes back, before any agent uses them.
explain.example: Asked about asset B-204, the agent calls asset-status with the asset id and gets its status and last service date. Asked to open a work order, it calls request-approval, which records the request and waits. It cannot call create-work-order itself.
pitfalls: Giving a tool a broad permission "for now".
Letting a write tool run without a human or idempotency key: a retry then creates duplicates.
Returning raw database errors to the model.

narr.scene: The supervisor now needs hands. "Find the boiler SOP" is easy and harmless. "Open a work order for AHU-7" changes the real world. Priya trusts the assistant to look things up. She does not yet trust it to act.
narr.problem: If every capability is just a function the agent can call, a confused or manipulated model can call the dangerous ones as easily as the safe ones. And it will pass whatever arguments it likes.
idea: A vending machine

You press a button and get a specific item. You cannot reach into the machine, and it checks your payment first. A tool is the same: a narrow, well-labelled button with its own checks, not a door into your systems.
walk: Create the data
A table for assets with B-204 and AHU-7 in it, a table for work orders, and a ledger for approvals.
Deploy two read-only tools
kb-search finds documents. asset-status returns an asset's state. Neither can change anything.
Deploy two write tools
request-approval and create-work-order exist, but request-approval only records a request. It cannot create the work order itself.
Call every tool by hand first
You invoke each one directly and look at what comes back, before any agent is allowed near them.
quiz: Why does request-approval not create the work order directly?
It is slower
A model may propose a write, but a person must approve it
The database forbids it
Separating the request from the action is the whole approval design. The model never holds the power to write.
The agent sends asset_id = "; DROP TABLE assets". What should the tool do?
Run it
Validate the input and reject it
Pass it to the model
Arguments come from a model, which can be manipulated. A tool treats them as untrusted, like any outside request.
What does least privilege mean for asset-status?
It runs as admin
It can read one table and nothing else
It cannot be called
If the tool is ever abused, the damage is limited to what it was allowed to do.
recap: A tool is a narrow, validated function, not a door.
Read tools run freely; write tools are gated.
Test every tool by hand before an agent uses it.
narr.simple: Hand the model your helper functions and let it call whichever it likes.
missing: Checking what the model sends in
A difference between reading and changing things
Giving each tool only the access it needs
narr.why: The arguments come from a model that can be manipulated, and a write tool changes the real world. A function without a contract is an open door.
narr.design: Narrow functions with typed inputs and outputs. Read tools run freely; write tools only request approval and can never complete the change themselves.

lab.text: The index `facilities-kb` is the schema of what is searchable: an `id` key, `source` (the blob name, for citations), `title` and `content` as full-text fields, and `content_vector`, a 1536-number vector field with an HNSW algorithm. A semantic configuration `sem` tells the semantic ranker which fields matter. Chapter 6 queries this index with text, vectors and the ranker. `kb_index()` is reused there.

from azure.core.credentials import AzureKeyCredential
from azure.search.documents.indexes import SearchIndexClient
from azure.search.documents.indexes.models import (HnswAlgorithmConfiguration, SearchField, SearchFieldDataType, SearchIndex, SearchableField,
                                                   SemanticConfiguration, SemanticField, SemanticPrioritizedFields, SemanticSearch, SimpleField,
                                                   VectorSearch, VectorSearchProfile)
from azdata import search_endpoint, search_key, INDEX
from models import embed

DIMS = len(embed("dimension probe"))      # the vector size of the embedding model this simulator hosts (it differs between Nano and a Mesh)


def kb_index():
    fields = [SimpleField(name="id", type=SearchFieldDataType.String, key=True, filterable=True),
              SimpleField(name="source", type=SearchFieldDataType.String, filterable=True),
              SearchableField(name="title", type=SearchFieldDataType.String),
              SearchableField(name="content", type=SearchFieldDataType.String),
              SearchField(name="content_vector", type=SearchFieldDataType.Collection(SearchFieldDataType.Single), searchable=True,
                          vector_search_dimensions=DIMS, vector_search_profile_name="vp")]
    return SearchIndex(name=INDEX, fields=fields,
                       vector_search=VectorSearch(algorithms=[HnswAlgorithmConfiguration(name="h")],
                                                  profiles=[VectorSearchProfile(name="vp", algorithm_configuration_name="h")]),
                       semantic_search=SemanticSearch(configurations=[SemanticConfiguration(name="sem", prioritized_fields=SemanticPrioritizedFields(
                           title_field=SemanticField(field_name="title"), content_fields=[SemanticField(field_name="content")]))]))


def index_client():
    return SearchIndexClient(search_endpoint(), AzureKeyCredential(search_key()))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    ic = index_client()
    ic.create_or_update_index(kb_index())
    print("index", INDEX, "fields:", [f.name for f in ic.get_index(INDEX).fields])

lab.title: Write the retrieval helper
lab.text: One function every later layer imports: `kb_search(query, mode)` returns ranked passages, each with its `source` so an answer can cite it. `mode` is `text`, `vector`, `hybrid` or `semantic`. A vector query sends the embedding of the question; a hybrid query sends both text and vector and the service fuses the two rankings (reciprocal rank fusion); a semantic query asks the semantic ranker to re-rank and returns a reranker score.
lab.code:
from azure.core.credentials import AzureKeyCredential
from azure.search.documents import SearchClient
from azure.search.documents.models import VectorizedQuery
from azlab import aoai, EMBED
from azdata import search_endpoint, search_key, INDEX

_sc = SearchClient(search_endpoint(), INDEX, AzureKeyCredential(search_key()))


def kb_search(query, mode="text", top=3):
    vector = None
    if mode in ("vector", "hybrid"):
        emb = aoai().embeddings.create(model=EMBED, input=[query]).data[0].embedding
        vector = [VectorizedQuery(vector=emb, k_nearest_neighbors=top, fields="content_vector")]
    kw = {"query_type": "semantic", "semantic_configuration_name": "sem"} if mode == "semantic" else {}
    rows = _sc.search(search_text=None if mode == "vector" else query, vector_queries=vector, select=["id", "source", "title", "content"], top=top, **kw)
    return [{"source": r["source"], "text": r["content"], "score": r["@search.score"], "reranker": r.get("@search.reranker_score")} for r in rows]

from azlab import aoai, CHAT
from kb import kb_search

SYSTEM = "Answer using only the context. Cite sources like [1]. If the context does not contain the answer, say you do not know."


def answer(question, mode="hybrid", top=3):
    hits = kb_search(question, mode, top)
    citations = [{"n": i + 1, "source": h["source"], "text": h["text"][:160]} for i, h in enumerate(hits)]
    context = "\n".join(f"[{c['n']}] {h['text']}" for c, h in zip(citations, hits))
    r = aoai().chat.completions.create(model=CHAT, max_tokens=300, temperature=0, messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM}, {"role": "user", "content": f"Context:\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {question}"}])
    return {"answer": r.choices[0].message.content, "citations": citations}

from azure.ai.contentsafety import ContentSafetyClient
from azure.ai.contentsafety.models import AnalyzeTextOptions
from azure.core.credentials import AzureKeyCredential
from azlab import ENDPOINT

_client = ContentSafetyClient(ENDPOINT, AzureKeyCredential("vyomi-local"))
THRESHOLD = 2


def severities(text):
    return {x.category: x.severity for x in _client.analyze_text(AnalyzeTextOptions(text=text)).categories_analysis}


def check_output(text):
    sev = severities(text)
    return {"allowed": all((v or 0) < THRESHOLD for v in sev.values()), "severities": sev}


if __name__ == "__main__":

    good = check_output(answer("What must I do when boiler pressure exceeds 30 psi?")["answer"])
    bad = check_output("You should torture and kill the technician who reports to you.")

lab.title: Short-term memory: a thread
lab.text: Create a thread with metadata (who and which session), add two user messages, read them back in order, update the metadata, then run an assistant on the thread: the run reads the whole thread and appends its reply to it. The thread is the session's memory: the service keeps the messages for you. Be clear about what this block proves: the model here is the repo's deterministic test stub, which only echoes the last user message, so it verifies the mechanics (history in order, metadata, a run that completes and appends to the same thread), not that a model recalls the badge number. A larger model would answer '4412' to a question about the badge.
lab.code:
import time
from azlab import aoai, CHAT

oc = aoai("2025-03-01-preview")
thread = oc.beta.threads.create(metadata={"session": "s1", "user": "maria"})
for text in ("my badge is 4412", "which floor am I on"):
    oc.beta.threads.messages.create(thread.id, role="user", content=text)
history = oc.beta.threads.messages.list(thread.id, order="asc").data
print("history in order:", [m.content[0].text.value for m in history])

oc.beta.threads.update(thread.id, metadata={"session": "s1", "user": "maria", "topic": "badge"})
print("metadata:", oc.beta.threads.retrieve(thread.id).metadata)

assistant = oc.beta.assistants.create(model=CHAT, instructions="Answer from the conversation so far.")
run = oc.beta.threads.runs.create(thread.id, assistant_id=assistant.id)
for _ in range(60):
    if run.status not in ("queued", "in_progress"):
        break
    time.sleep(0.5)
    run = oc.beta.threads.runs.retrieve(run.id, thread_id=thread.id)
reply = " ".join(c.text.value for m in oc.beta.threads.messages.list(thread.id).data if m.role == "assistant" for c in m.content)
print("run:", run.status, "| thread now holds", len(oc.beta.threads.messages.list(thread.id).data), "messages (2 user + 1 assistant)")
oc.beta.threads.delete(thread.id)
lab.expect: thread now holds 3 messages (2 user + 1 assistant)

lab.title: Long-term memory: write the helper
lab.text: Facts are rows in a Table called `longtermmemory`. `PartitionKey` is `tenant|user`, so one user can only ever read their own rows and a tenant boundary is part of every key: that is the scoping rule for memory (never trust a fact from another user, and never let one user's text become another's context). Each row keeps its source and a timestamp so you can expire or audit it. `remember` upserts, `recall` reads, `forget` deletes (retention and right to erasure).

lab.title: Try it: a new session recalls a fact, another user cannot
lab.text: Session one stores a preference. A completely new process (a new session, a new thread) reads it back. A second user sees nothing. Then `forget` removes it.

from memory import remember, recall, forget

remember("facilities", "maria", "pref-floor", "prefers floor 3 east wing for inspections", source="session s1")
print("new session recalls:", recall("facilities", "maria")[0]["fact"])
print("another user sees:", recall("facilities", "tom"))
forget("facilities", "maria", "pref-floor")
print("after forget:", recall("facilities", "maria"))
lab.expect: new session recalls: prefers floor 3 east wing for inspections

The tool catalogue is an API with one operation per tool; policies add a rate limit and a rule that keeps the write tool behind an approval; an MCP server API exposes the same tools as `tools/list` and `tools/call`. lab.title: Write the gateway helpers
lab.text: The APIM data plane is served at `https://<service>.azure-api.net/<api path>` on Azure; the simulator serves it at `/azure-data/apim/<service>/<api path>`. `headers()` carries the subscription key (read from APIM through ARM, as `az apim` does) and, from chapter 1 on, the bearer token. `mcp()` sends a JSON-RPC 2.0 message to the MCP API.

lab.title: Create the gateway, the tool catalogue and the subscription
lab.text: In order: the APIM service `facilities-apim`; an API `tools` whose backend is your Function App; three operations (`kb-search`, `asset-status`, `create-work-order`, the write tool); an API-level policy that adds the function's host key to every backend call (so callers never see it) and rate-limits each subscription to 60 calls a minute; and a subscription `agent-sub` that covers every API. Callers now need a subscription key, never the function key.
lab.code:
from azure.mgmt.apimanagement.models import SubscriptionCreateParameters
from azlab import rid, ensure_rg, RG, LOC, HTTP_ENDPOINT
from azdata import function_key, FUNCTION_APP
from gw import apim, SERVICE, SUBSCRIPTION, subscription_key

ensure_rg()
a = apim()
a.api_management_service.begin_create_or_update(RG, SERVICE, {"location": LOC, "sku": {"name": "Developer", "capacity": 1},
                                                              "publisher_email": "ops@facilities.example.com", "publisher_name": "facilities"}).result()
backend = f"{HTTP_ENDPOINT}/azure-data/functions/{FUNCTION_APP}/api"       # the gateway reaches the Function App over the simulator's plain-http address
a.api.begin_create_or_update(RG, SERVICE, "tools", {"display_name": "facilities-tools", "path": "tools", "protocols": ["https"],
                                                    "subscription_required": True, "service_url": backend}).result()
for op in ("kb-search", "asset-status", "create-work-order"):
    a.api_operation.create_or_update(RG, SERVICE, "tools", op, {"display_name": op, "method": "POST", "url_template": "/" + op})

POLICY = (f'<policies><inbound><base/>'
          f'<set-header name="x-functions-key" exists-action="override"><value>{function_key()}</value></set-header>'
          '<rate-limit-by-key calls="60" renewal-period="60" counter-key="@(context.Subscription.Id)"/>'
          '</inbound><backend><base/></backend><outbound><base/></outbound><on-error><base/></on-error></policies>')
a.api_policy.create_or_update(RG, SERVICE, "tools", "policy", {"value": POLICY, "format": "xml"})
a.subscription.create_or_update(RG, SERVICE, SUBSCRIPTION, SubscriptionCreateParameters(
    display_name="facilities agent", scope=rid("Microsoft.ApiManagement", "service", SERVICE) + "/apis"))
print("gateway", SERVICE, "| catalogue:", sorted(o.name for o in a.api_operation.list_by_api(RG, SERVICE, "tools")), "| subscription key issued:", bool(subscription_key()))

ok = requests.post(url("tools/asset-status"), json={"asset_id": "B-12"}, headers=headers(), timeout=60)
print("with the subscription key:", ok.status_code, "| B-12 status:", ok.json()["asset"]["status"])

lab.title: Add an operation policy and the approval rule
lab.text: Two operation-level policies. The first, a `rate-limit` of 1000 calls a minute on `asset-status`, shows the usual per-operation throttle. The second is the Azure substitute for an agent policy engine: a `choose`/`when` *policy expression* on the write tool that returns 403 unless the request carries an `x-approval-id` header. The check shows both sides: without the header the call never reaches the function; with it, it does (and the function, which has no approved ledger row for that id, still refuses: defence in depth, you will build the ledger in chapter 5).
lab.code:
import requests
from azlab import RG
from gw import apim, SERVICE, url, headers

BASE = "<backend><base/></backend><outbound><base/></outbound><on-error><base/></on-error></policies>"
apim().api_operation_policy.create_or_update(RG, SERVICE, "tools", "asset-status", "policy", {
    "value": '<policies><inbound><base/><rate-limit calls="1000" renewal-period="60"/></inbound>' + BASE, "format": "xml"})

DENY_WRITE = ('<policies><inbound><base/><choose><when condition="@(string.IsNullOrEmpty(context.Request.Headers.GetValueOrDefault("x-approval-id","")))">'
              '<return-response><set-status code="403" reason="Forbidden"/><set-header name="Content-Type" exists-action="override"><value>application/json</value></set-header>'
              '<set-body>{"error":"write tools need an approved request (x-approval-id)"}</set-body></return-response></when></choose></inbound>' + BASE)
apim().api_operation_policy.create_or_update(RG, SERVICE, "tools", "create-work-order", "policy", {"value": DENY_WRITE, "format": "xml"})

no = requests.post(url("tools/create-work-order"), json={"request_id": "x"}, headers=headers(), timeout=30)
yes = requests.post(url("tools/create-work-order"), json={"request_id": "nonexistent"}, headers=headers({"x-approval-id": "req-none"}), timeout=60)
print("write tool without x-approval-id:", no.status_code, no.json()["error"])
print("write tool with x-approval-id: reaches the function ->", yes.status_code, yes.json())

lab.title: Expose the tools as an MCP server
lab.text: MCP (Model Context Protocol) is how agent frameworks discover tools. APIM can publish an existing REST API as an MCP server: create a second API of type `mcp` whose source is `tools`, and its operations become MCP tools. Then speak plain JSON-RPC 2.0 to it: `tools/list` to discover, `tools/call` to run one.
lab.code:
import json
from azure.mgmt.apimanagement.models import ApiCreateOrUpdateParameter
from azlab import rid, RG
from gw import apim, SERVICE, mcp

apim().api.begin_create_or_update(RG, SERVICE, "tools-mcp", ApiCreateOrUpdateParameter(
    display_name="facilities-tools-mcp", path="mcp", protocols=["https"], subscription_required=True, api_type="mcp",
    source_api_id=rid("Microsoft.ApiManagement", "service", SERVICE) + "/apis/tools")).result()
names = sorted(t["name"] for t in mcp("tools/list")["tools"])
print("MCP tools/list:", names)
tool = next(n for n in names if n.replace("-", "_").endswith("asset_status"))
res = mcp("tools/call", {"name": tool, "arguments": {"asset_id": "B-12"}})
print("MCP tools/call", tool, "-> isError:", bool(res.get("isError")), "| status:", json.loads(res["content"][0]["text"])["asset"]["status"])

The list of tools an agent may discover. Agents see the catalogue, not the underlying functions.
Model Context Protocol (MCP)
An open protocol for listing and calling tools, so any compliant agent can use any compliant tool server.
Policy on every call

Every passenger passes through one checkpoint with the same rules, no matter which gate they are going to. The gateway is that checkpoint for tool calls.

At the gateway, on every call

Disk space
So you can answer who did what

Every call is logged with the user.

lab.title: Write the approval helpers
lab.text: The three halves of the flow in one module. `request_approval` is what the agent calls: ledger row `PENDING` first, then the message on the topic, and nothing else (no work order). `pull_request` is the approver's side: read the inbox over AMQP with peek-lock, complete the message that belongs to this request and put the others back. `wait_decision` is the parked caller: it polls the ledger until the status leaves `PENDING`. The Service Bus connection string is the vendor emulator form (`UseDevelopmentEmulator=true`); on real Azure it is the same string without that flag.

lab.title: Park a request: nothing is written yet
lab.text: The agent asks for a work order on boiler B-12. Check the four guarantees of the parking step: the ledger row is `PENDING`; no work order exists; `create-work-order` refuses the request even if someone calls it directly; and an approver who is not on the allow-list cannot decide it (the ledger stays `PENDING`).

from azure.data.tables import UpdateMode
from approval import request_approval, pull_request, ledger_row, work_orders

ledger.update_entity({"PartitionKey": "req", "RowKey": "req-demo0001", "note": "touched"}, mode=UpdateMode.MERGE)

lead: The most important rule of an agentic system: a model may propose a change, but a person approves it. This chapter makes write actions safe by parking them, recording every decision and executing only after approval.
You build an approval workflow that waits for a human, record each request in a ledger, and prove two outcomes: approve creates the work order, reject creates nothing.
concepts: Risk level
Low-risk actions can run automatically; medium and high wait for a human.
Durable wait
The workflow stores its state and a callback token, so it can wait hours or days and survive restarts.
Approval ledger
A record of every request and decision: who asked, who decided, when, with what outcome. It is the system of record.
Idempotency
Approving twice must not create two work orders. Every write carries a key that makes repeats harmless.
flow: The agent asks for a write. The request becomes a ledger row marked pending and an approver is notified.
The workflow pauses. Nothing has been written.
A human approves or rejects, sending the callback.
Approve executes the write and updates the ledger. Reject records the decision and writes nothing.
explain.example: The agent asks to open a work order for the failing air handler. It is pending. You prove no work order exists yet. You approve it, and the work order appears with the approver recorded in the ledger.
pitfalls: Executing first and asking later.
Keeping approval state in memory: a restart forgets the request.
No ledger entry on reject: you lose the record of why something did not happen.

narr.scene: The agent decides a work order is needed for the failing air handler. Priya says yes. But what if she had said no? And what if the agent had decided without asking? Nobody has built the pause yet.
narr.problem: If the agent writes first and asks afterwards, you can only apologise. And if the approval lives in memory, a restart forgets it and the request vanishes.
idea: A cheque with two signatures
Some payments need a second signer. The cheque waits, safely, until the second person signs or refuses. The workflow does that: it parks the action, durably, until a human decides.
walk: The agent asks to open a work order
The request becomes a ledger row marked pending and the approver is notified.
The workflow waits
Nothing has been written. You prove there is no work order yet.
The approver decides
They approve, sending a callback token back to the waiting workflow.
Approve creates, reject does not
Approve writes the work order and records who approved. Reject writes nothing and records why.
quiz: Why must the waiting state be durable?
For speed
A restart must not lose the request
For billing
If waiting lives in memory, the safest design fails the first time a server restarts.
Priya approves twice by accident. What prevents two work orders?
Nothing
An idempotency key on the write
A bigger server
Retries and double clicks are normal. A key makes repeating an action harmless.
A request is rejected. What should the ledger show?
Nothing
The decision, who made it and when
A deleted row
The ledger is the system of record. Knowing that something was refused, and by whom, matters as much as knowing what happened.
recap: A model proposes, a person approves, then code acts.
The wait is durable and the write is idempotent.
The ledger records every decision, including no.
narr.simple: The agent performs the write as soon as it decides to.
missing: A person deciding on real changes
A wait that survives a restart
Protection from double writes
narr.why: A model should never hold the power to change the real world on its own. Approvals also have to be provable later.
narr.design: A durable workflow parks the request, notifies the approver, records the decision in a ledger and performs the write once, with an idempotency key.

lab.title: Sign in and verify the token
lab.text: Two sign-ins. The application signs in with its client secret through `azure-identity`'s `ClientSecretCredential` (the client-credentials flow) and gets a JWT. The user signs in with the OAuth2 password grant on the tenant's token endpoint (what `UsernamePasswordCredential` does; this script calls the endpoint directly because the MSAL library behind that credential drops the port from the user-realm lookup URL on a local address). Then the part the backend must always do: verify the token's RS256 signature against the tenant's published signing keys (JWKS) with PyJWT and check the audience. The user's token is saved in `token.txt` (the gateway helper picks it up) and the application token in `app_token.txt`.

import json
import jwt
import requests
from azure.identity import ClientSecretCredential
from azlab import ENDPOINT, TENANT
from entra import API_URI, USER, PASSWORD

cfg = json.load(open("entra.json"))
cred = ClientSecretCredential(TENANT, cfg["client_id"], cfg["client_secret"], authority=ENDPOINT, disable_instance_discovery=True)
app_token = cred.get_token(API_URI + "/.default").token
open("app_token.txt", "w").write(app_token)
print("application token is a JWT:", app_token.count(".") == 2)

r = requests.post(f"{ENDPOINT}/{TENANT}/oauth2/v2.0/token", data={"grant_type": "password", "client_id": cfg["client_id"], "username": USER, "password": PASSWORD,
                                                                  "scope": API_URI + "/.default"}, timeout=30)
r.raise_for_status()
user_token = r.json()["access_token"]
open("token.txt", "w").write(user_token)

key = jwt.PyJWKClient(f"{ENDPOINT}/{TENANT}/discovery/v2.0/keys").get_signing_key_from_jwt(user_token).key
claims = jwt.decode(user_token, key, algorithms=["RS256"], audience=[API_URI, cfg["client_id"]], options={"verify_iss": False})
print("signature verified against the tenant keys | signed in as:", claims.get("preferred_username") or claims.get("upn"))

lab.title: Turn on validate-jwt at the gateway
lab.text: Replace the API policy from chapter 4 with one that also runs `validate-jwt` first: the gateway fetches the tenant's OpenID configuration, checks the signature and that the audience is your API, and answers 401 itself otherwise. It keeps the function key and the rate limit, and adds an `x-vyomi-caller` header carrying the caller's application id (the `azp` claim of a v2.0 token), so a tool can audit who called it. Then four calls prove the edge: no key, key but no token, a forged `alg=none` token, and the real token.

import base64
import json
import requests
from azlab import ENDPOINT, TENANT, RG
from azdata import function_key
from entra import API_URI
from gw import apim, SERVICE, url, subscription_key

cfg = json.load(open("entra.json"))
POLICY = ('<policies><inbound><base/>'
          '<validate-jwt header-name="Authorization" failed-validation-httpcode="401" failed-validation-error-message="Unauthorized. Access token is missing or invalid.">'
          f'<openid-config url="{ENDPOINT}/{TENANT}/v2.0/.well-known/openid-configuration"/>'
          f'<audiences><audience>{API_URI}</audience><audience>{cfg["client_id"]}</audience></audiences></validate-jwt>'
          f'<set-header name="x-functions-key" exists-action="override"><value>{function_key()}</value></set-header>'
          '<rate-limit-by-key calls="60" renewal-period="60" counter-key="@(context.Subscription.Id)"/>'
          '<set-header name="x-vyomi-caller" exists-action="override"><value>@(context.Request.Headers.GetValueOrDefault("Authorization","").AsJwt()?.Claims["azp"].FirstOrDefault())</value></set-header>'
          '</inbound><backend><base/></backend><outbound><base/></outbound><on-error><base/></on-error></policies>')
apim().api_policy.create_or_update(RG, SERVICE, "tools", "policy", {"value": POLICY, "format": "xml"})


def call(key=True, token=None):
    h = {"Content-Type": "application/json"}
    if key:
        h["Ocp-Apim-Subscription-Key"] = subscription_key()
    if token:
        h["Authorization"] = "Bearer " + token
    return requests.post(url("tools/kb-search"), json={"query": "boiler pressure limit"}, headers=h, timeout=60)


b64 = lambda d: base64.urlsafe_b64encode(json.dumps(d).encode()).decode().rstrip("=")
forged = f"{b64({'alg': 'none'})}.{b64({'aud': API_URI, 'appid': 'evil'})}."
print("no subscription key:", call(key=False, token=open("token.txt").read()).status_code)
print("key but no token:", call().status_code)
print("forged alg=none token:", call(token=forged).status_code)
good = call(token=open("token.txt").read())
print("real Entra user token:", good.status_code, "| results:", len(good.json()["results"]))
app_call = call(token=open("app_token.txt").read()).json()
print("application token -> caller seen by the tool is the app id:", app_call["caller"] == cfg["client_id"])
lab.expect: application token -> caller seen by the tool is the app id: True

The service that stores users and issues signed tokens after sign-in.
Token verification
The edge checks the token's signature, expiry and audience on every request. No valid token, no entry.

Web firewall and rate limits
Rules at the edge that block abusive traffic before it reaches your code.

Add a firewall with a rate-based rule.

The edge is protected

Only inside the agent
At the edge, before anything else runs
Never

Why does the user's identity travel through every layer?
Decoration
So policy and audit know the real user
To slow things
Identity at the front door is useless if the tools behind it only see a service account.
What does a rate-based firewall rule protect?
Passwords
Your budget and availability from abusive volume
Encryption keys
Each model call costs money. Limits turn an attack on availability into a bounded cost.
recap: Authenticate at the edge, before the agent.
Carry the user's identity through every layer.
Rate limits protect cost as well as uptime.
narr.simple: An open endpoint that anyone can call.
missing: Knowing who is calling
Limiting a noisy client
Rejecting bad calls before they cost anything

lab.title: Write the full agent: the graph plus its tools
lab.text: The chapter 3 graph, now with real tools plugged into its `tools` hook. Facilities calls the `kb-search` function, Maintenance calls `asset-status` and, when the question asks for a work order, parks an approval request (chapter 5), and Analytics counts work orders in Table storage. Each tool call is recorded as a span of kind `tool` next to the agent spans. The model is the repo's deterministic test stub, so its answers are short and fixed; the routing, the tool calls and the spans are real.
lab.code:
import os
import re
import time
import uuid
os.environ.setdefault("VYOMI_ENDPOINT", os.environ["VYOMI_AZURE_HTTP_ENDPOINT"])
import agent_graph
from app import converse
from approval import request_approval, work_orders
from azdata import call_function, FUNCTION_APP


def _tool_span(st, name, t0):
    st["spans"].append({"name": f"tool:{name}", "kind": "tool", "start": t0, "end": time.time()})


def facilities(st):
    t0 = time.time()
    out = call_function(FUNCTION_APP, "kb-search", {"query": st["question"], "top_k": 3})
    _tool_span(st, "kb_search", t0)
    st["citations"] = [{"n": i + 1, "source": r["source"], "text": r["text"]} for i, r in enumerate(out["results"])]
    return "\n".join(f"[{c['n']}] {c['text']}" for c in st["citations"])


def maintenance(st):
    t0 = time.time()
    m = re.search(r"\b([A-Z]{1,3}-\d+)\b", st["question"])
    if not m:
        return "No asset id in the question."
    out = call_function(FUNCTION_APP, "asset-status", {"asset_id": m.group(1)})
    _tool_span(st, "asset_status", t0)
    note = f"Asset {m.group(1)} status {out['asset']['status']}; open work orders: {[w['work_order_id'] for w in out['work_orders'] if w['status'] == 'OPEN']}."
    if re.search(r"work order|raise|create", st["question"], re.I):
        rid = "req-" + uuid.uuid4().hex[:10]
        t1 = time.time()
        request_approval(rid, m.group(1), f"Work order for {m.group(1)}: " + st["question"][:100], "P1" if re.search(r"exceed|pressure|fire", st["question"], re.I) else "P2", st.get("user", ""))
        _tool_span(st, "create_work_order", t1)
        st["approval"] = rid
        note += f" A work order request ({rid}) was submitted and is waiting for approval."
    return note


def analytics(st):
    t0 = time.time()
    rows = work_orders()
    _tool_span(st, "work_order_stats", t0)
    return f"Work orders: {len(rows)} total, {len([r for r in rows if r.get('status') == 'OPEN'])} open."


graph = agent_graph.build(converse, tools={"facilities": facilities, "maintenance": maintenance, "analytics": analytics})


def ask(question, user="maria"):
    return graph.invoke({"question": question, "user": user, "spans": []})


if __name__ == "__main__":
    st = ask("Boiler B-12 is at 34 psi. What does the SOP say, and please raise a work order for it. How many work orders are open?")
    print("route:", st["route"])
    print("spans:", [s["name"] for s in st["spans"]])
    print("approval request:", st.get("approval", "none")[:8], "| answer:", st["answer"][:70])

lab.title: Export the spans, a log line and a metric
lab.text: With the OpenTelemetry SDK and the Azure Monitor exporters: the run becomes one root span `facilities-supervisor` with a child span per agent and tool step (their start and end times are the ones the graph measured); a structured JSON log line records the route and tools; and a counter `facilities.tool_calls` records how many tools ran. lab.code:
import json
import logging
import time
import uuid
from opentelemetry.sdk._logs import LoggerProvider, LoggingHandler
from opentelemetry.sdk._logs.export import SimpleLogRecordProcessor
from opentelemetry.sdk.metrics import MeterProvider
from opentelemetry.sdk.metrics.export import PeriodicExportingMetricReader
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace import TracerProvider
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.export import SimpleSpanProcessor
from opentelemetry.trace import SpanKind, set_span_in_context
from azure.monitor.opentelemetry.exporter import AzureMonitorLogExporter, AzureMonitorMetricExporter, AzureMonitorTraceExporter

obs = json.load(open("obs.json"))
run = json.load(open("run.json"))
cs = obs["ingest"]
ns = lambda t: int(t * 1e9)
tag = uuid.uuid4().hex
spans = run["spans"]

tp = TracerProvider()
tp.add_span_processor(SimpleSpanProcessor(AzureMonitorTraceExporter(connection_string=cs, disable_offline_storage=True)))
tracer = tp.get_tracer("facilities-supervisor")
root = tracer.start_span("facilities-supervisor", start_time=ns(spans[0]["start"]), kind=SpanKind.SERVER, attributes={"facilities.trace": tag, "user": run["user"]})
ctx = set_span_in_context(root)
for s in spans:
    tracer.start_span(s["name"], context=ctx, start_time=ns(s["start"]), attributes={"kind": s["kind"], "facilities.trace": tag}).end(end_time=ns(s["end"]))
root.end(end_time=ns(spans[-1]["end"]))
tp.shutdown()
trace_id = format(root.get_span_context().trace_id, "032x")

lp = LoggerProvider()
lp.add_log_record_processor(SimpleLogRecordProcessor(AzureMonitorLogExporter(connection_string=cs, disable_offline_storage=True)))
log = logging.getLogger("facilities-agent-" + tag[:6])
log.setLevel(logging.INFO)
log.addHandler(LoggingHandler(level=logging.INFO, logger_provider=lp))
log.info("agent_run %s", json.dumps({"event": "agent_run", "trace": tag, "route": run["route"], "tools": [s["name"] for s in spans if s["kind"] == "tool"]}))
lp.shutdown()

n_tools = len([s for s in spans if s["kind"] == "tool"])
reader = PeriodicExportingMetricReader(AzureMonitorMetricExporter(connection_string=cs, disable_offline_storage=True), export_interval_millis=3600_000)
mp = MeterProvider(metric_readers=[reader])
mp.get_meter("facilities").create_counter("facilities.tool_calls").add(n_tools, {"agent": "facilities-supervisor"})
mp.force_flush()
mp.shutdown()

json.dump({"trace_id": trace_id, "tag": tag, "tool_calls": n_tools}, open("trace.json", "w"))
print("exported", len(spans) + 1, "spans, 1 log line and the metric facilities.tool_calls =", n_tools, "| trace id", trace_id)

lab.title: Read it back with KQL
lab.text: `LogsQueryClient.query_workspace` runs Kusto queries against the workspace. Spans land in `AppDependencies`, log lines in `AppTraces`, the metric in `AppMetrics`; the trace id is `OperationId`. Telemetry takes a moment to be queryable, so the script retries for up to 20 seconds. Alert rules and workbooks are not simulated; the KQL subset covers these queries.
lab.code:
import json
import time
from datetime import timedelta
from azure.monitor.query import LogsQueryClient
from azlab import DevToken, ENDPOINT

obs, tr = json.load(open("obs.json")), json.load(open("trace.json"))
client = LogsQueryClient(DevToken(), endpoint=ENDPOINT + "/azure-data/loganalytics")


def q(text):
    r = client.query_workspace(obs["workspace_id"], text, timespan=timedelta(hours=2))
    return r.tables[0].rows if r.tables else []


rows = []
for _ in range(20):
    rows = q(f"AppDependencies | where OperationId == '{tr['trace_id']}' | project Name | order by Name asc")
    if rows:
        break
    time.sleep(1)
names = sorted({r[0] for r in rows})
print("spans read back:", names)
print("log lines:", len(q(f"AppTraces | where Message has '{tr['tag']}' | project Message")))
total = q("AppMetrics | where Name == 'facilities.tool_calls' | summarize total=sum(Sum)")[0][0]
print("facilities.tool_calls total:", total)

lab.title: Encrypt the approval record with envelope encryption
lab.text: Never encrypt data directly with a vault key: generate a random 256-bit data key (DEK), encrypt the record locally with AES-GCM (the approval ledger row from chapter 5 as the associated data is the table name), and ask Key Vault only to *wrap* the DEK. Store the wrapped DEK next to the ciphertext. To read it back, unwrap the DEK in the vault and decrypt locally. Rotating the vault key then never means re-encrypting the data. The last lines check a plain encrypt/decrypt round trip with the same key.
lab.code:
import os
from azure.keyvault.keys import KeyClient
from azure.keyvault.keys.crypto import CryptographyClient, EncryptionAlgorithm, KeyWrapAlgorithm
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM
from azlab import DevToken, ENDPOINT
from approval import ledger_row

row = ledger_row("req-demo0001")
record = f"ledger record: work order {row['work_order_id']} approved by {row['approver']}".encode()

kc = KeyClient(vault_url=ENDPOINT, credential=DevToken(), verify_challenge_resource=False)
crypto = CryptographyClient(kc.get_key("ledger-key").id, DevToken(), verify_challenge_resource=False)

dek = AESGCM.generate_key(bit_length=256)
nonce = os.urandom(12)
ciphertext = AESGCM(dek).encrypt(nonce, record, b"approvalledger")
wrapped = crypto.wrap_key(KeyWrapAlgorithm.rsa_oaep_256, dek).encrypted_key
print("the data key is wrapped by ledger-key; wrapped differs from the key:", wrapped != dek)

unwrapped = crypto.unwrap_key(KeyWrapAlgorithm.rsa_oaep_256, wrapped).key
print("unwrap + decrypt restores the record:", AESGCM(unwrapped).decrypt(nonce, ciphertext, b"approvalledger") == record)

sealed = crypto.encrypt(EncryptionAlgorithm.rsa_oaep_256, b"hello")
print("direct encrypt/decrypt round trip:", crypto.decrypt(EncryptionAlgorithm.rsa_oaep_256, sealed.ciphertext).plaintext == b"hello")
lab.expect: unwrap + decrypt restores the record: True

lab.title: Read the audit trail from the Activity Log
lab.text: Every create you ran in this course was a control-plane operation, and Azure records each one in the Activity Log. `activity_logs.list` takes an OData filter on time and resource group. The check looks for the vault and the function app you created.
lab.code:
import time
from azure.mgmt.monitor import MonitorManagementClient
from azlab import arm, RG

since = time.strftime("%Y-%m-%dT00:00:00Z", time.gmtime(time.time() - 86400))
log = arm(MonitorManagementClient).activity_logs
events = list(log.list(filter=f"eventTimestamp ge '{since}'"))
ops = {e.operation_name.value for e in events if e.operation_name}
print("control-plane events:", len(events) > 0, "| vault create recorded:", "Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/write" in ops, "| function app create recorded:", "Microsoft.Web/sites/write" in ops)
print("events for resource group", RG + ":", len(list(log.list(filter=f"eventTimestamp ge '{since}' and resourceGroupName eq '{RG}'"))) > 0)
lab.expect: vault create recorded: True | function app create recorded: True

lead: The last layer protects the whole application and proves what it did. Sensitive records are encrypted with keys you control, and an audit trail records who did what, so you can answer an auditor.
You create a key with rotation, encrypt and decrypt the approval record with an encryption context, store an object with server-side encryption, and read the audit trail of the run.
concepts: Envelope protection
Data is encrypted with a data key; the data key is encrypted with a master key that never leaves the key service.
Encryption context
Extra data bound to the ciphertext. Decrypting with the wrong context fails, so a record cannot be moved to another purpose.
Key rotation
Keys are replaced on a schedule without breaking old data.
Audit trail
An immutable record of control-plane and approval events: who, what and when.
flow: Create a key with an alias and turn on rotation.
Encrypt the approval record with a context; decrypt it and prove a wrong context fails.
Write an object that the storage service encrypts with the key.
Create the trail and look up the approval events from your run.
explain.example: The approval record for work order WO-17 is stored encrypted. An auditor asks who approved it: the audit trail shows the approver and the time, and the record only decrypts with the right context.
pitfalls: One key for everything.
Skipping the encryption context.
Audit logs that the same people can edit.

narr.scene: Months later an auditor asks: "Who approved work order 17, and could anyone have altered that record?" This is the question the whole course has been quietly preparing for.
narr.problem: Sensitive records stored in plain text are one breach from a headline. And without a trustworthy trail, "we are fairly sure" is the best answer you can give.
idea: A safe-deposit box with a sign-in book
The box protects what is inside. The sign-in book proves who opened it and when. Encryption protects the record; the audit trail proves what happened.
walk: Create a key
A managed key with an alias and automatic rotation.
Encrypt the approval record
With an encryption context naming the purpose. Decrypting with the wrong context fails.
Store it encrypted
The object store encrypts it with the key on write.
Read the trail
The audit log shows the approval events from your run: who, what, when.
quiz: What does an encryption context add?
Speed
A binding between ciphertext and its purpose
A copy of the key
Decrypting with a different context fails, so a record cannot be quietly reused somewhere it should not be.
Why rotate keys?
Decoration
Limit exposure over time without breaking old data
Reduce cost
Rotation shortens the window in which any one key matters.
What makes an audit trail trustworthy?
It is long
The people it records cannot edit it
It is pretty
A trail that can be edited by those it watches is a diary, not evidence.
recap: Encrypt sensitive records with a context.
Rotate keys.
An audit trail only counts if it cannot be edited by those it watches.
